newsitem.title: JAPAN: Ex-PM Hata quits main Japan opposition party.
newsitem.headline: Ex-PM Hata quits main Japan opposition party.

text.p: In a big blow to Japan's largest opposition party, former prime minister Tsutomu Hata and 12 followers quit Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) on Thursday and set up a new political group.
"To carry on the same dead-end course will put Japan on the road to ruin," Hata told a news conference after founding the new party, called Taiyoto (Sun Party).
The long-expected defection follows bitter squabbling between Hata and Shinshinto leader and longtime political ally Ichiro Ozawa since the party made a poor showing in general elections in October.
The two lawmakers, who spent decades in the ruling Liberal Democratic Party before quitting the LDP in 1993 and founding Shinshinto in 1994, disagreed over how to oppose their former party.
"This is a better step than continuously bickering within the party," Hata told reporters after the resignations.

Although he smiled and shook hands with Hata for television cameras, Ozawa told reporters the defectors had "betrayed the expectations of all of us in Shinshinto, whose support enabled them to win in the last general elections."
Hata said his new party, made up mostly of former LDP lawmakers, would work with Shinshinto and other opposition parties to promote economic and administrative reforms.
"We share similar objectives to promote reform and I would like to maintain cooperative ties," Hata said.
The new party's platform, which calls for streamlining the bureaucracy and carrying out fiscal reform, was little different from that of Shinshinto, analysts said.

The Sun Party and the Democratic Party, formed in September by popular former health minister Naoto Kan, had agreed to regular policy consultations before parliament convenes next month, media reports said.
Some political observers have said the Hata group could launch a new wave of political realignment in Japanese politics following two years of relative calm after splits in the LDP in 1993 and 1994.

But other observers, including LDP officials, welcomed the breakup of the largest opposition party and predicted that other Shinshinto lawmakers would follow, with some perhaps joining the ruling camp.
"Our door has always been open," said LDP Secretary General Koichi Kato said.
Before elections in October, five Shinshinto lawmakers rejoined the LDP, prompting expectations of a mass exodus.

The fractious Shinshinto was the product of the merger of nine political groups that formed the core of the reformist coalition governments that broke the LDP's 38-year grip on power and ruled briefly in 1993 and 1994.
Shinshinto has spent much of its time and energy overcoming factionalism and has been unable to inspire voters or capitalise on unpopular government policies.
In the October general elections it captured 156 seats, far behind the LDP's 239 in the 500 seat Lower House of parliament.

Hata was prime minister for two months before he was ousted in June 1994 and replaced by an LDP-dominated coalition headed first by Socialist prime minister Tomiichi Murayama and, since last January, by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
